# Graphing Best Practices {#sec-graphing-principles}

A chart takes a table of numbers and turns it into something a reader can take in at a glance.
A good test of whether it is working is to ask whether the reader would have understood the
data faster from the table itself.  A good chart tells you the story immediately.  A bad one
makes you work through the axes, the labels and the legend before you can see what should have
been obvious.

Let me illustrate with two charts.  @fig-minard is what @tufte concludes "might well be
the best statistical graphic ever drawn".  The figure, whose text is in French, documents the
advance and subsequent retreat of Napoleon's army into Russia.  The width of the main line
denotes the size of Napoleon's forces, the horizontal axis represents the geography of Russia,
while the bottom line graph denotes the temperature.  The tan band is the army marching east
and the black band is what came back: 422,000 men crossed the Polish border and 10,000
returned.  You can read the disasters off it directly -- at the Berezina river crossing the
black band halves, and the temperature line below it reads -30° Réaumur, about -37 Celsius.
I can take issue with the size of the labels in the graph, but one cannot deny the ominous
story that it tells.

![Charles Joseph Minard, *Carte figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l'Armée
Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812--1813* (1869).  Public domain.  Click to view it
full size.](images/minard.png){#fig-minard}

The second chart, @fig-georgia, was published by the Georgia Department of Public Health in
May 2020.  It shows confirmed COVID-19 cases in the state's five worst-affected counties over
a fifteen-day window, and the story it appears to tell is a steady decline.

![Georgia Department of Public Health, "Top 5 Counties with the Greatest Number of Confirmed
COVID-19 Cases," May 2020.  Reproduced from the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law
[@sabin2020georgia].  Click to view it full size.](images/georgia_covid.png){#fig-georgia}

However, when you read the dates along the bottom you will find that they are not-sequential -- the graph is sorted by case count not by date.  The story this graph imparts is wrong and it's only when the reader strains to read every element of the graph does can some semblance of truth emerge.

The state did not defend the design.  A spokesperson for the governor's office said: "The x
axis was set up that way to show descending values to more easily demonstrate peak values and
counties on those dates.  Our mission failed.  We apologize.  It is fixed."

Hopefully, we can learn to create graphs that more are more like @fig-minard rather than @fig-georgia.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

- Say what question a chart is supposed to answer before you build it
- Choose a chart type that suits the comparison you are making
- Label a chart so a reader who did not make it can read it
- Spot the common ways a chart misleads, and avoid them in your own work
:::

## The Principles {#sec-chart-principles}

Before we get into specific chart types, some general principles. These come from a long tradition of work on data visualization, especially by Edward Tufte (*The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*) and more recently by Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic (*Storytelling with Data*):

- **Don't use a chart if you don't need one.**  A chart earns its place when there is a
  pattern in the data that prose cannot carry.  With two numbers there is no pattern, only two
  numbers, and a sentence does the job: *in 2024 the United States produced 53.7 million tonnes
  of wheat and Canada produced 34.9 million.*  A chart of those two figures asks the reader to
  measure two bars to recover what the sentence already told them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wheat-two
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.0
#| fig-height: 1.5
#| fig-cap: "Two numbers do not need a chart."
source("R/chart_types.R")
fig_wheat(2)
```

  Now ask a question with a shape to it -- where does Canada sit among the world's wheat
  producers? -- and the chart starts doing work no sentence can.

```{r}
#| label: fig-wheat-fifteen
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 3.4
#| fig-cap: "The top fifteen wheat producing countries, 2024/25. Canada highlighted. Approximate figures from USDA."
fig_wheat(15)
```

  You can see at once that Canada is fifth, that the top three are in a different league, and
  that Canada and Australia are close enough to trade places in a bad year.  Writing that out
  would take a paragraph, and the reader still would not see it.

- **Be honest.** As with the case of the Georgia covid case counts above, charts can deceive as much as they can illuminate.  Methods of deception include: a) sorting data  .  Humans minds try to recognize patterns and assign meaning -- if we see dates on the horizontal axis, we expect them to be in sequential order.  If we see one bars on a chart, we expect their relative size to be representative of something.

    Truncating an axis is the commonest version.


Both panels show the same five malting barley varieties, which yield between 103 and 114
bushels.

```{r}
#| label: fig-truncated
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.6
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-cap: "The same five yields: axis at 100, and axis at zero."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "A. Axis starting at 100"
#|   - "B. Axis starting at zero"
#| layout-ncol: 2
source("R/chart_types.R")
fig_truncated(ymin = 100, labels = FALSE)
fig_truncated(ymin = 0)
```

Panel A has no numbers on the bars, so there is nothing to check the heights against.  Starting
the axis at 100 means the bars show yield *minus one hundred*: CDC Copeland's 3 sits next to
AAC Synergy's 14, and a 10% gap becomes a bar four times taller.  Nothing is fabricated, which
is what makes it both effective and dishonest.  Check where the axis starts before you read
anything else.

- **Graphs need *descriptive* titles and labels.**  Label both axes, noting the units were applicale. In Excel, add these from **Chart Design → Add Chart Element → Chart Title** and **→ Axis Titles**. Missing labels are the most common problem in student charts.  Note that if you are embedding the chart in a Word document, it is generally better to put a title or caption in Word itself, rather than using the Excel built-in title.

- **Minimize clutter.**  Some charts are embellished with 3d effects, shadows, patterned fills, or tick marks.  Usually these are just distracting noise.  Ruthlessly remove noise that does not tell the story of the data.



Panel A has a tick every 5 bushels, gridlines in both directions, a marker on every point,
a drop shadow behind every line, a shaded panel and a boxed legend.  Panel B has the same
four series.

```{r}
#| label: fig-clutter
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.7
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-cap: "The same four series, cluttered and decluttered."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
source("R/chart_types.R")
fig_clutter(load_yields())
fig_declutter(load_yields())
```

Patterned fills come from an era when charts were printed in black and white and hatching
was the only way to tell one bar from another.  On a screen they shimmer.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pattern
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.7
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-cap: "Patterned fills, and the same bars filled flat."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
fig_pattern(load_yields())
fig_flat(load_yields())
```

A 3D bar or pie chart tilts the plane, so bars at the front read larger than identical bars
at the back and you can no longer line a bar up against the axis.

- **Label directly when possible.** A chart where each line is labeled at the end is easier to read than one with a legend that forces the eye to jump back and forth.



Below are the same barley variety shares drawn both ways.  Try finding Newdale in each.

::: {layout-ncol=2}
![A. Direct labels](images/variety_shares_direct_labels.png)

![B. Legend](images/variety_shares_legend.png)
:::

- **Use text on the chart, sparingly.** If a reader is going to stop at something and wonder
  why, a few words on the plot save them the trip to the caption.  One note answering the
  obvious question is usually enough; a chart annotated at every turn is back to being
  cluttered.

```{r}
#| label: fig-annotated
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-cap: "Spring wheat yields, with the one thing a reader would ask about named on the plot."
fig_annotated(load_yields())
```

- **A chart can carry more than two variables, up to a point.** Position on the two axes is
  what the eye reads best, but it is not all you have.  The size of a point, its colour, its
  shape: each can carry another variable.  Minard's map manages six.  Below is the scatter of
  wheat against barley yields from earlier, with the acres seeded in each zone added as the
  size of the point.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bubble
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 5.4
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-cap: "Three variables: wheat yield, barley yield, and acres as the size of the point."
fig_bubble(load_yields())
```

  The extra variable answers a question the plain scatter could not: the zones at the top right
  are not just the highest yielding, they are also where most of the wheat is grown.  Size
  works here because it is only being asked to rank -- big, medium, small -- and not to be read
  off precisely.

  What does not work is giving a chart two different vertical scales, one on the left and one
  on the right.  Both panels below plot canola yield and canola acres over the same five years,
  and the only difference between them is how the right-hand axis was scaled.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dual
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-cap: "The same two series, with the right-hand axis scaled two different ways."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
fig_dual_axis(load_yields(), TRUE)
fig_dual_axis(load_yields(), FALSE)
```

  In A the lines cross in 2022 and acres appear to run ahead of yield.  In B they barely meet.
  Nothing in the data changed.  Where two series cross, which one looks higher, and whether one
  seems to lead the other are all decided by a choice of scale that the reader cannot see and
  the author may not have thought about.  Plot the two series in separate panels instead, or
  put one of them on an index.

- **Use colour purposefully.** Colour is not just decoration!  It can be used to convey information. Colour can also be used to draw the reader's attention to a particular finding (though one should avoid misusing this power!) or to express intensity.


- **Be wary of pie charts.** Most books on visual display are pretty hostile to pie charts.  One reason is that it it is much more difficult to compare the size of angles to the size of bars.  See below the pie chart of the vote share in the 2021 Canadian election.  It is kind of hard to immediately see that the Conservatives gained more votes than the Liberals in the pie chart.  Much easier in the bar chart.  Of course you can also put the percentages directly in the pie chart -- but then why not simply use a table?

```{r}
#| label: fig-vote
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-cap: "Popular vote share in the 2021 Canadian federal election. Source: Elections Canada."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
fig_vote("pie")
fig_vote("bar")
```

## Types of Charts {#sec-chart-types}

Most of the work in making a good chart is picking the right kind in the first place.  The
choice follows from the comparison you want the reader to make, so it helps to state that
comparison out loud before you open a chart menu.  All the figures below are drawn from the
same Saskatchewan variety data, so you can see how differently the same numbers read.

```{r}
#| label: setup-charts
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
source("R/chart_types.R")
yields <- load_yields()
```

### Bar charts: comparing categories {.unnumbered}

A bar chart compares a value across categories -- yields by crop, acres by region, revenue by
customer.  The eye is good at judging the length of a bar against its neighbours, which is why
bar charts do so much of the work in practice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| fig-cap: "A bar chart compares one value across categories."
fig_bar(yields)
```

Two habits make bar charts better.  Sort the bars by size unless the categories have their own
natural order, because a sorted chart answers "which is biggest?" instantly and an
alphabetical one makes the reader hunt.  And start the axis at zero.  A bar encodes its value
by length, so cutting the axis at 30 makes a 5% difference look like a doubling.  This is the
single most common way a chart misleads, and it is usually the software's default rather than
anyone's intent.

Note that the chart above runs horizontally.  Most people reach for vertical bars by default,
which is fine when the labels are short, but category names are often long -- variety names,
regions, product lines -- and vertical bars leave no room for them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bar-orientation
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 4.4
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-cap: "The same five varieties, vertical and horizontal."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
fig_bar_vertical()
fig_bar_horizontal()
```

In panel A the names have to be rotated to fit, so the reader tilts their head and the labels
take up a third of the plot.  In panel B they sit on their own line, horizontal and left
aligned, and the chart can hold twenty categories as comfortably as five.  Turn the chart on
its side whenever the labels are longer than a word or two.

### Line charts: change over time {.unnumbered}

A line chart shows how something moves over a continuous scale, almost always time.  The line
implies the values connect, which is exactly why you should not use one for categories: a line
running from Barley to Canola to Oats suggests a progression that does not exist.

```{r}
#| label: fig-line
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-cap: "A line chart shows movement over time. Labelling each line at its right-hand end saves the reader a trip to the legend."
fig_line(yields)
```

Unlike bar charts, line charts do not need a zero baseline.  Nothing is encoded by length, so
you are free to zoom in on the range where the action is -- but say so, and do not zoom so far
that ordinary variation looks like a crisis.

### Scatter plots: the relationship between two variables {.unnumbered}

A scatter plot puts one variable on each axis and a point at every observation.  Use it when
you want to know whether two things move together.

```{r}
#| label: fig-scatter
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.4
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-cap: "A scatter plot asks whether two variables move together. Each point is one of Saskatchewan's 21 risk zones."
fig_scatter(yields)
```

Each point is a risk zone, with its wheat yield on one axis and its barley yield on the other.
The points run up and to the right, which says a zone that grew good wheat that year generally
grew good barley too -- unsurprising, since both crops got the same rain.  A scatter showing
*no* pattern would be just as informative.

This is the workhorse of statistical analysis and it returns in Module 4, where we put a line
through the cloud and start measuring how strong the relationship is.

### Stacked bars: parts of a whole {.unnumbered}

A stacked bar breaks each bar into components, showing both the total and its composition.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stacked
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-cap: "A stacked bar shows the total and its composition at once."
fig_stacked(yields)
```

The catch is that only the bottom segment sits on a common baseline.  You can compare canola
acres across years easily because they all start at zero; comparing the middle segments means
judging the length of a floating block, which the eye does poorly.

### Grouped bars {.unnumbered}

The obvious fix is to unstack the bars and set them side by side, so every bar starts at zero.

```{r}
#| label: fig-grouped
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 2.9
#| fig-cap: "The same acres, grouped rather than stacked."
fig_grouped(yields)
```

This solves the baseline problem and introduces a different one.  There are now twenty bars,
and the chart supports two comparisons at once: across crops within a year, and across years
within a crop.  The second is the one you usually want, and it is the harder of the two --
following canola from 2021 to 2025 means jumping over three other bars at every step.  The
grouping does not help; it is in the way.

Grouped bars work when there are only two or three series and few categories, so the eye can
take in a group at once.  Past that they get busy quickly.  When you find yourself building
one, it is worth asking whether the chart is really several charts.  Splitting it into a small
panel per crop gives each series its own baseline and its own space:

```{r}
#| label: fig-facet
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| fig-cap: "The same acres again, one panel per crop."
fig_facet(yields)
```

These are called **small multiples**, and they scale in a way that grouped bars do not: twelve
crops would be twelve panels, still readable, where twelve series in a grouped bar chart would
be unusable.  The trade is that comparing exact values across panels is harder, so use them
when the shape of each series matters more than ranking them against each other.

### Pie charts: use sparingly {.unnumbered}

A pie chart shows shares of a total.  It is the most criticized chart type in the field, and
the reason is worth seeing rather than taking on faith.  @fig-pie shows the same four numbers
twice.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pie
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 3.4
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| fig-cap: "The same four numbers, twice."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - ""
#|   - ""
#| layout-ncol: 2
pv <- fig_pie_vs_bar(yields)
pv$pie
pv$bar
```

In panel A, how much bigger is canola than spring wheat?  Most people guess a much wider gap
than the real one, because the eye judges angle and area poorly.  Panel B gives you 47% and
38% directly, and the answer takes no work at all.  The pie is not useless -- it does convey
"canola is about half the acres" at a glance -- but any comparison finer than that is easier
in a bar chart.

If you use one, keep it to a handful of slices, label them directly, and never make it 3D.  A
3D pie tilts the plane, which makes the near slices larger than the far ones for no reason but
decoration.

### Histograms and box plots {.unnumbered}

These two describe the distribution of a single variable rather than comparing categories, and
you met them in @sec-charts.  A histogram bins the values and shows the shape; a box plot
compresses that shape into a median, a box holding the middle half of the data, and whiskers.
Reach for them when the question is about spread rather than comparison.

### Choosing {.unnumbered}

The short version:

| If the question is | Use |
|---|---|
| How does this value compare across categories? | Bar chart |
| How has this changed over time? | Line chart |
| Are these two variables related? | Scatter plot |
| What is this total made of? | Stacked bar, or a bar chart of the components |
| How does each of several series move? | One panel per series |
| How is a single variable distributed? | Histogram or box plot |

When a chart does not obviously fit one of these, that is often a sign the question is not
sharp enough yet.

## Excel vs R for Charts {#sec-excel-vs-r-charts}

I want to be honest about this: **Excel charts are fine for many purposes.** They are easy to make, they look acceptable with default settings, and they are immediately editable by non-technical colleagues. If you are making a one-off chart for an internal meeting, Excel may be the right choice.

R (ggplot2) wins when you need:

- The chart to be reproducible from a script.
- The chart to update automatically as the underlying data changes.
- Many similar charts (via faceting or loops).
- Fine-grained control over appearance.
- Statistical features (trend lines, confidence bands, quantile ribbons).

Most working analysts use both. In this course we will lean on R, because reproducibility is the harder habit to pick up later.
